claims.text: In situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction enables real-time monitoring of oxidation kinetics under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
In situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction enables real-time monitoring of phase transformations under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The proposed starting material is an initially unoxidized metal alloy or coating with a well-defined room-temperature crystalline structure.
The experiment combines controlled oxidation from ambient temperature to approximately 1200°C with continuous high-flux synchrotron XRD acquisition.
A constant oxygen flow such as 50 mL/min promotes oxidation during heating to approximately 1200°C.
Synchrotron XRD patterns can be acquired at approximately 1 second per frame under the proposed conditions.
Oxidation proceeds through evolving oxide phases and transient crystalline intermediates.
High synchrotron photon flux provides sufficiently rapid crystallographic data to capture the onset and evolution of oxidation and phase changes.
In situ synchrotron XRD overcomes temporal delays and other limitations of conventional ex situ characterization.
The method will reveal rapid oxidation-product formation and transient phases that slower ex situ methods cannot detect.
Changes in diffraction-peak positions or intensities will correlate with oxidation progression.
Ex situ oxidation studies analyze samples only after cooling and may therefore miss dynamic phase transformations.
The method is applicable only when oxidation and phase-transformation time scales are resolvable at a 1-second frame rate.
Processes substantially faster than the acquisition time can fall outside the method's applicability.
Materials susceptible to synchrotron beam damage can fall outside the method's applicability.
Sensitivity and temporal resolution for very short-lived transient phases depend on the material and experimental setup.
Quantitative oxidation kinetics inferred by the method can vary with material type and experimental setup.
